title: The daily prayer for open doors
hookLine: for decades the Ardas asked for free access to the gurdwaras left behind

lines: A DOOR YOU CAN'T WALK THROUGH.
A LONGING PUT INTO A PRAYER.
cards: A childhood house someone else lives in now. A grandparent's town across an ocean. A front door remembered exactly, that can't be walked through.
For Sikhs after 1947, that door was Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, and many other gurdwaras now across a border. The community didn't keep that longing for one anniversary a year.
It put it into the prayer said every day.

teach.b: You've met the Ardas already: the standing prayer that closes nearly every Sikh gathering, said hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib.

It remembers the ten Gurus, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, and then it asks. It isn't a fixed text from one day in history; its core is old, and the community has added to it as the story went on.
After Partition, a request was added.
In plain English, it asks the Guru to grant the Khalsa free sight of, and the care and service of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated.
The Punjabi phrase at its heart is khulle darshan didar: open sight, open visits. So ever since, in homes and gurdwaras around the world, Sikhs have asked every day for a door to open.

teach.h: A LOSS TURNED INTO DAILY HOPE.
teach.b: A loss that could have turned bitter became a daily hope, said out loud, together. The door was not fully shut.

Groups of pilgrims, called jathas, were allowed to cross for the big gurpurabs, under agreements between India and Pakistan. But for many Sikhs, a visit to Guru Nanak's birthplace stayed a lifelong hope.
Many never went, and still the line was said.
The request is in the Ardas today, because Sikhs still ask for open, free access to all the places they were separated from.
It's a small lesson in holding a longing: not by forgetting it, not by letting it harden, but by praying it, gently, every day.

how: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of most Sikh gatherings, Sikhs ask for open access to, and the care of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras from which the Panth was separated in 1947.

games.q: your community has lost access to its holiest places. how does the Sikh community carry that loss?
o: stop mentioning the places, so it hurts less.
add a request for them to the daily prayer.
remember them only on one day a year.
games.why: a request was added to the Ardas, so the hope is said aloud every day, in gurdwaras and homes worldwide.

practice: Let one long hope come to mind: a reconciliation, a healing, a place you want to see, a door you want opened, for you or for someone else. Don't push it or plan it; just let it be there.
If you pray, offer it in your own words, the way the Sikh community has offered its hope for decades; if you don't, name it quietly to yourself and notice how long you've carried it.
